title: The Longer Cold Water Trial
text:
In a study published in 1993, Daniel Kahneman, Barbara Fredrickson, Charles Schreiber and Donald Redelmeier asked volunteers to hold one hand in painfully cold water, at about 14 degrees Celsius, in two separate trials.

In the short trial, the hand stayed in the cold water for 60 seconds. In the long trial, it stayed for the same 60 seconds at 14 degrees, and then for 30 more seconds while the researchers quietly let slightly warmer water flow in, raising the temperature by about one degree. The water was still uncomfortable, but a bit less so. The long trial therefore contained everything in the short one, plus extra time in pain.

Afterwards, participants were told they would have to repeat one of the two trials and could choose which. About two thirds chose to repeat the long one. They preferred more total pain because its ending was less bad, and they remembered the long trial as less unpleasant overall.

The result fit what Kahneman called the peak-end rule: when we remember an experience, we judge it mainly by its most intense moment and by how it ended, and we largely ignore how long it lasted. A related study by Redelmeier and Kahneman found the same pattern in patients' memories of colonoscopies. The gap between the experiencing self and the remembering self became a central theme of Kahneman's later work.
lesson: People remember an experience by its high point and its ending more than its length. When you host, teach, treat or serve someone, put special care into how it ends.
people: Daniel Kahneman, Barbara Fredrickson, Charles Schreiber, Donald Redelmeier
source: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., and Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6), 401-405.
